```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

tidycarbon measures the electricity your machine draws while R code runs and
converts it to an emissions estimate. The measuring is done by
[CodeCarbon](https://codecarbon.io), which is installed automatically through
reticulate the first time you create a tracker.

There are two ways to use a tracker:

- **Around a script.** `tracker_start()` and `tracker_stop()` open and close
  one window around whatever runs in between.
- **Around a function.** `carbon_track()` and `carbon_track_all()` run a
  function for you and return its result together with what it cost, one tidy
  row per call.

This guide uses both on the text of Jane Austen's novels, then compares two
ways of scoring sentiment. The output shown is from a real run.

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidycarbon)
library(dplyr)
library(tidytext)
library(janeaustenr)

books <- austen_books() |>
  mutate(docid = paste0(book, "_", row_number()))

books
#> # A tibble: 73,422 × 3
#>    text                    book                docid
#>    <chr>                   <fct>               <chr>
#>  1 "SENSE AND SENSIBILITY" Sense & Sensibility Sense & Sensibility_1
#>  2 ""                      Sense & Sensibility Sense & Sensibility_2
#>  3 "by Jane Austen"        Sense & Sensibility Sense & Sensibility_3
#> # ℹ 73,419 more rows

count_words <- function(data) {
  data |>
    unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
    count(book, word, sort = TRUE)
}
```

## Track a script

Create a tracker with `carbon_init()`, start it, run your code, and stop it.
Nothing in between needs to change:

```{r}
tracker <- carbon_init(project_name = "austen", measure_power_secs = 1)

tracker_start(tracker)
word_counts <- count_words(books)
emissions <- tracker_stop(tracker)

emissions
#> [1] 6.157096e-06
```

`tracker_stop()` returns the emissions of the window in kgCO2eq. The full
record is appended to `emissions.csv` in your working directory, one row per
window:

```{r}
read.csv("emissions.csv") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(project_name, duration, energy_consumed, emissions, cpu_model)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   project_name duration energy_consumed  emissions cpu_model
#>   <chr>           <dbl>           <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 austen           3.60       0.0000162 0.00000616 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700K
```

`measure_power_secs` is how often CodeCarbon samples power. The default of 10
seconds suits long jobs; for code that finishes in a few seconds, set it to 1.

## Track a function

`carbon_track()` takes a function, its arguments and a tracker. It calls the
function and returns one row holding the result and the measurement:

```{r}
tracker <- carbon_init(project_name = "austen", measure_power_secs = 1)

res <- carbon_track(count_words, data = books, tracker = tracker)

res |> select(fun, task_id, duration, energy_consumed, emissions_total)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   fun         task_id                              duration energy_consumed emissions_total
#>   <chr>       <chr>                                   <dbl>           <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1 count_words 9dec149d-9baa-431e-b84c-b7d0a3393524    0.437       0.0000198      0.00000754
```

`duration` is in seconds, `energy_consumed` in kWh and `emissions_total` in
kgCO2eq. The function's own return value is in the `result` list-column:

```{r}
res$result[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 40,378 × 3
#>    book              word      n
#>    <fct>             <chr> <int>
#>  1 Mansfield Park    the    6206
#>  2 Mansfield Park    to     5475
#>  3 Mansfield Park    and    5438
#> # ℹ 40,375 more rows
```

The energy is also split by component. At this scale watt-hours and
milligrams are easier to read than kWh and kg:

```{r}
res |>
  transmute(
    cpu_wh   = cpu_energy * 1000,
    gpu_wh   = gpu_energy * 1000,
    ram_wh   = ram_energy * 1000,
    total_wh = energy_consumed * 1000,
    co2e_mg  = emissions_total * 1e6
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    cpu_wh gpu_wh  ram_wh total_wh co2e_mg
#>     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 0.00675 0.0106 0.00242   0.0198    7.54
```

Every row also records the hardware and location the measurement came from,
so results from different machines stay distinguishable:

```{r}
res |>
  select(country_name, cpu_model, cpu_count, gpu_model,
         ram_total_size, codecarbon_version) |>
  glimpse()
#> Rows: 1
#> Columns: 6
#> $ country_name       <chr> "Germany"
#> $ cpu_model          <chr> "13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700K"
#> $ cpu_count          <int> 24
#> $ gpu_model          <chr> "1 x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 Ti"
#> $ ram_total_size     <dbl> 62.58013
#> $ codecarbon_version <chr> "3.3.1"
```

## Compare two approaches

Is a dictionary-based sentiment score cheaper with tidytext or with quanteda?
Write each as a function of the same data:

```{r}
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.sentiment)

tidy_sentiment <- function(data) {
  data |>
    unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
    inner_join(get_sentiments("afinn"), by = "word",
               relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    group_by(docid) |>
    summarise(sentiment = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))
}

quanteda_sentiment <- function(data) {
  corp <- corpus(data, text_field = "text", docid_field = "docid")
  textstat_valence(corp, dictionary = data_dictionary_AFINN)
}
```

`carbon_track_all()` takes a list of tasks, each a function and its
arguments, and tracks them one after another on the same tracker:

```{r}
tasks <- list(
  list(fun = tidy_sentiment,     args = list(data = books)),
  list(fun = quanteda_sentiment, args = list(data = books))
)

runs <- carbon_track_all(tasks, tracker)

runs |>
  transmute(fun, duration,
            energy_wh = energy_consumed * 1000,
            co2e_mg   = emissions_total * 1e6)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   fun                duration energy_wh co2e_mg
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 tidy_sentiment        0.443    0.0193    7.35
#> 2 quanteda_sentiment    0.868    0.0420   16.0
```

The result is one row per task, in the order you gave them, with the
function's name in `fun`. A single run of half a second is a noisy
measurement, so repeat the tasks and summarise:

```{r}
carbon_track_all(rep(tasks, 5), tracker) |>
  group_by(fun) |>
  summarise(runs = n(),
            duration  = median(duration),
            energy_wh = median(energy_consumed) * 1000)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   fun                 runs duration energy_wh
#>   <chr>              <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 quanteda_sentiment     5    0.867   0.0253
#> 2 tidy_sentiment         5    0.329   0.00911
```

Before reading the tidytext version as the cheaper way to get the same answer,
look at what each returned:

```{r}
nrow(runs$result[[1]])
#> [1] 33165
nrow(runs$result[[2]])
#> [1] 73422
```

tidytext drops every line without a dictionary word; quanteda scores all
73,422 lines and gives those a 0. A comparison of cost only means something
once the two functions do the same job.

## How to read the numbers

- **Energy is measured where the hardware allows it.** Here the CPU is read
  from RAPL counters and the GPU from the NVIDIA driver; RAM is estimated
  from its size. CodeCarbon prints which method it used when the tracker is
  created. Where no counter is available it falls back to an estimate from
  the CPU model.
- **Emissions are derived.** They are the energy multiplied by a carbon
  intensity for the location in `country_name`, not a second measurement.
- **It is the whole machine.** A browser or another job running at the same
  time is counted too. Close what you can and repeat short measurements.

## Where next

- `carbon_run()` tracks a whole pipeline as one expression, `carbon_step()`
  each step of it, and `carbonbench()` benchmarks two expressions against
  each other; see
  `vignette("pipelines-and-benchmarks")`.
- For code that calls a hosted language model, the work happens at the
  provider; see `vignette("remote-tracking")`.
